newsitem.title: CHINA: GM to break ground for China joint venture.
newsitem.headline: GM to break ground for China joint venture.

text.p: General Motors will this week formally break ground for a new $1.57 billion joint venture in Shanghai that will help the U.S. car giant crack the tough Chinese market, company officials said on Wednesday.

The new venture, which will turn out a mid-sized Buick Regal sedan model, would help GM get a foothold in China's tightly protected domestic market, said Rudolph Schlais, president of General Motors China.

Shanghai General Motors (SGM) would start producing cars in April 1999 and was aiming for eventual production of 100,000 cars a year to try to win much of the important government and corporate segment, Schlais said.
"For the next five years (the market) is basically going to be institutional buyers," Schlais said in an interview at the 1997 Shanghai International Automobile Industry Exhibition.
"That's going to be 90-95 percent of the market," Schlais told Reuters.
The venture, split 50-50 between GM and Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp, would officially break ground on Thursday and could eventually make cars for export to other Asian countries, he said.
"Our whole objective is to be in China to increase market share in Asia-Pacific," he said. "The first focus will be on the domestic market."
But Schlais and other industry officials said China's car demands would change as nearly two decades of capitalist-style reforms lifted more of the country's 1.2 billion people into the middle class.
If China eased restrictions on consumer credit in the car industry, sales of utilitarian models would soar, he said.
China produced about 1.6 million motor vehicles last year, including about 400,000 passenger cars. Forecasts have put total production at 2.7 million by 2000.

GM was trying to expand its presence in China by working on a light truck deal in Shenyang in the northeastern province of Liaoning, and by seeking a stake in a south China plant being abandoned by French car maker Peugeot, Schlais said.

GM has said it wants to produce a smaller, Opel model car at the Peugeot Guangzhou plant aimed at the lower end of the market where industry analysts say the bulk of future private ownership will lie.
"We are having discussions and negotiations with the Guangzhou municipal government," Schlais said but declined to give further details about any possible deal.
"Our objective is to have more activities and be a player in the China auto market based upon the Chinese needs," he said.
Another joint venture with light truck-maker FAW-Jinbei in Liaoning had been set up in late 1992 but the two sides were yet to agree on a product, he said.
The Shanghai-made Buicks were designed to go head-to-head with foreign-made Mercedes and BMWs that were now subject to import tariffs of 100-120 percent, he said.
Schlais said Shanghai GM could still compete even if those high tariffs were drastically reduced as part of China's bid to enter the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

"We're looking very closely at what will happen with the tariffs, realising that one of the criteria of WTO will be tariff reduction," he said, adding GM supported China's eventual entry into the global free trade club.
